content: The process of developing the Country Cooperation Strategy (CCS) involves six distinct stages, which are outlined in Figure 2 and elaborated upon in the CCS Guide. A prototype CCS document is available as a supplementary resource to the guide, serving as a template to assist countries in creating their own CCS. This guide is applicable to all countries receiving technical assistance from the World Health Organization (WHO), regardless of whether the organization has a dedicated Country Office or provides support through another country or Regional Office. The guide is designed to be flexible, accommodating countries in conflict or fragile situations as well as high-income nations, enabling them to adopt a similar approach. The CCS should reflect the priorities of the respective country, aligning with the Thirteenth General Programme of Work (GPW13) and the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF) timeframe. Ideally, it should contribute to the health component of the Country Common Analysis (CCA) and UNSDCF. Conversely, the CCA/UNSDCF should ideally inform the CCS. This phase is closely linked to the evaluation process, which provides critical input for the development of a new CCS. Key considerations when preparing a new CCS include findings from the evaluation of the previous CCS, as well as UNSDCF evaluations. The evaluation phase outlines how these inputs can guide the CCS development process. External factors, such as upcoming elections, political instability, civil unrest, or humanitarian crises, should also be taken into account. The six stages of the CCS cycle begin with Stage 1, which involves analyzing the country context. Where a WHO Country Office (WCO) exists, the WHO Representative (WR) is responsible for leading the CCS process, ensuring its quality, and overseeing its implementation, monitoring, and reporting. All three levels of the WHO organization should be involved in the CCS development process, with the WR playing an active role throughout. In countries without a WCO, the Regional Country Support Unit (CSU) Office leads the process, with technical support from relevant units and headquarters as needed. The alignment of the CCS with the UNSDCF is critical. Ideally, the UNSDCF should be developed first to inform the CCS. If this is not feasible, the two can be developed in parallel. The prerogative lies with the country, and WHO ensures that the CCS aligns with the country’s needs and the UN process at the national level. The CCS is considered a UN instrument insofar as it reflects UNSDCF outcomes and includes additional standard-setting activities not prioritized in the UNSDCF. Early actions in the CCS development process include initial discussions with WCO staff, regional CSUs, and CSS/HQ, as well as consultations with key technical units and departments. Informal discussions with the Ministry of Health (MoH) and other relevant ministries are essential for gathering input and preparing stakeholders, including UN agencies, Resident Coordinators, and health and development partners, for active involvement. A CCS working group should be established, with its size depending on the country’s capacity. Additional expertise and resources should be identified if required. Networking with regional CSUs and CSS/HQ departments is crucial to access information, resources, guidance, and best practices. A robust evidence base is essential for developing a CCS that effectively addresses the country’s needs and supports its health-related Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) targets. Recent and disaggregated data are particularly important to ensure that health-related human rights and gender issues are adequately considered, and that vulnerable populations are not left behind. Disaggregated data strengthen evidence-based interventions at population, subpopulation, and individual levels, providing insights into gender-responsiveness, human rights-based, and equity-oriented approaches. The CCS should include a comprehensive analysis of the country context, covering political, social, demographic, economic, and environmental factors that impact health. This analysis should identify key drivers of progress, persistent challenges, health achievements, and areas of global and regional interest. Vulnerable populations and the legislative and policy environment affecting health should also be considered. For countries with an operational UN Country Team (UNCT), the country context analysis can be mapped from the CCA, particularly the section addressing the national context. The health and equity situation analysis should use GPW13 as the conceptual framework, tracking joint efforts by WHO and Member States to meet GPW13 targets. Baseline data for all indicators should be available at the inception of the CCS process, with national databases providing insights into health priorities and projections. Data should be disaggregated by sex, age, and other key measures to detect inequalities and guide evidence-based interventions. The CCS is a joint WHO-Member State instrument designed to facilitate the implementation of GPW13 and its triple billion targets: 1 billion more people benefiting from universal health coverage, 1 billion more people better protected from health emergencies, and 1 billion more people enjoying better health and well-being by 2023. The CCS defines strategic priorities and indicators to measure progress and impact, with countries selecting specific targets and indicators to track and evaluate milestones. The WHO Impact Framework, as outlined in Figure 3, provides a measurement system with three layers, including 46 programmatic indicators and milestones aligned with the SDGs. These indicators are disaggregated by key inequality measures to ensure relevance and focus on the country’s specific needs and challenges.
